newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain buries wage/price inflation spiral-analysts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain buries wage/price inflation spiral-analysts.

text.p: Britain has an inglorious inflation track record compared with Germany and France but many experts argue that the "wage/price" spiral which always struck in the past has been consigned to history.
A staggering fall in the numbers of jobless in Britain in January should be setting off all sorts of inflationary alarm bells if the boom-bust history of Britain's economy is anything to go by.
But the Conservative government, at least, sees no danger of high wage demands pushing retail prices through the roof.
This time it is different, the government says.

Angela Knight, economic secretary to the Treasury, said as much this month after the Office for National Statistics showed 67,800 people dropped off the unemployment registers in January, taking the number to a six-year low.
The unemployment rate has now tumbled to 6.5 percent from about eight percent a year ago.

"To say inflation is dead is premature but it's pretty ill," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International. "You have got to believe the evidence of your own eyes. Unemployment is at extremely low levels, historically, but inflation has not taken off."
Retail price figures, also released this month, showed underlying inflation -- which excludes home loan payments -- steady at 3.1 percent in the year to January.

That may be above the government's self-imposed target of 2.5 percent but is negligible compared with rampant periods of inflation in the 1970s and '80s which saw prices rising as much as 25 percent annually.

The experience of the last 50 years showed that as Britain's economy boomed and unemployment fell, a shortage of skilled workers forced wages higher and inflation rose. The rate of job creation now would certainly have fuelled inflation in the past.
But the government argues that the reams of labour legislation it pushed through in the 1980s has destroyed the ability of trade unions to force through hefty pay rises.
The culture of collective bargaining with powerful unions -- which did much to fuel the so-called "wage-price" spiral -- has been vanquished, it says.
SOME CREDIT BUT IT'S NOT ALL GOOD NEWS
Shepperd said the government can take some of the credit for the demise of wage-driven inflation. But he added that it was not all good news.

"They can take some of the credit but it's just as much job insecurity and paranoia that is keeping wages low and perhaps that is why the government trails in the polls when all the evidence points to a buoyant economy," he said.
Opinion polls show the ruling Conservative Party trailing opposition Labour by nearly 20 points with an election due within three months.

John Cridland, director of human resources at the employers' organisation, the Confederation of British Industry, said there was some evidence of a sea-change in the culture of wage settlements, not just forced by job insecurity.
"The CBI has gently suggested a new rationale is alive in the labour market and an environment of modest pay settlements is here to stay," he said.

CBI data suggest annual pay settlements average about 3.2 percent. In the 1980s, that average never dropped below five percent. "It's good news and surprising at this stage of the economic cycle," Cridland said.
In the past, economists have assumed that once the level of unemployment in Britain dropped below six percent or so, inflation would rear its ugly head.
PARALLEL WITH U.S.

But the parallel with the United States is instructive. There, the "inflation rate" of unemployment has generally been pegged around 5.5 to 6.0 percent. But the number of jobless has been below that for more than a year with no sign of inflation taking off.

The U.S. unemployment rate is 5.4 percent while consumer price inflation is running at three percent or so. "This is not just a UK phenomenon, it's a global one, where greater competition is keeping the lid on prices," Shepperd said.

On the other hand, Britain's labour market figures suggested wage pressures are not dead yet. The ONS said average earnings growth rose 4.25 percent in the year to December. November's earnings were revised up to 4.25, from 4.0 percent.

Bank of England chief economist Mervyn King told reporters that average earnings had risen by one percentage point over the past 12 months and warned if they continued at that rate for the next year, would threaten the government's inflation target.

But Shepperd backed the government's claim that the pick-up in earnings growth was driven by bonus payments, particularly to City fat cats in London's financial centre, rather than broad wage agreements. "The key issue is wage settlements", he said. "The Treasury is right to say they are not really going up."
Cridland at the CBI said the key factor was that wage increases should be justified by productivity increases, a credo the government has certainly pushed in the public sector.
"If manufacturing earnings growth of 4.75 percent reflects profitability and the rewards that result then that is all well and good," he said.

But he stopped short of heralding the demise of the wage-fuelled inflation. "We're hopeful but the jury remains out. You've got three years of good experience to set against 40 years of wage/price spiral."
